\newpage

**1. (30 points)** The variable biasnews is a Likert scale variable that measures a respondent’s agreement toward “News coverage about politics in America is biased.” Perform a one-sample t-test to determine whether the agreement toward this statement among all American adults is significantly less than 3, on average.

\medskip
**(a)** To make sense of this variable, look up its coding. A higher value for this variable corresponds to (choose one) less/more agreement toward the statement. What does a value of 3 (our test value) represent?


\medskip
**(b)** State the null and alternative hypotheses for this test.


\medskip
**(c)** Evaluate tenability of the normality assumption or indicate why the assumption is not an issue for this analysis.


\medskip
**(d)** Perform the t-test. p-value from Jamovi: _____. This is a one-sided/two-sided (choose one) p-value. Reject the null hypothesis (yes or no)? __________ Draw a conclusion of the test in the context of the question, using language that someone who didn’t know statistics and wasn’t familiar with the dataset would understand.


\medskip
**(e)** Report the effect size and give an interpretation in the context of the problem (make sure to mention the strength of the effect), or indicate why it is inappropriate to do so.


\medskip
**(f)** Report a 95% Confidence interval for the average agreement toward “News coverage about politics in America is biased” (biasnews) among all American adults.


\newpage

**2. (30 points)** Among American adults, is the average perception significantly different toward (1) the reliability of news on TV (tvnews1) and (2) the reliability of news on web (webnews)? Perform a paired samples t-test to find out.

\medskip
**(a)** The sample mean for tvnews1 is ________; the sample mean for webnews is ________. Based only on the sample means, which of the following is true? Hint: you might want to check the coding of the variables. Choose one:

- On average, people in the dataset think news on TV is more reliable.
- On average, people in the dataset think news on web is more reliable.
- On average, American adults think news on TV is more reliable.
- On average, American adults think news on web is more reliable.


\medskip
**(b)** State the null and alternative hypotheses for the paired samples t-test. If you write a notation with a generic subscript (e.g., $\mu_1$, $\bar{X}_2$), explain what the notation means in text.


\medskip
**(c)** Report the p-value of the test: ________. State your conclusion in the context of the problem, using language that someone who didn’t know statistics and wasn’t familiar with the dataset would understand.


\medskip
**(d)** Report and interpret the effect size, or state why we should not do this.


\medskip
**(e)** Report the 95% confidence interval of the mean difference.


\medskip
**(f)** Can we decide whether or not we should reject the null hypothesis based on the confidence interval above? If so, explain how. If not, explain why not.

**3. (15 points)** In this question, you are expected to conduct a thorough analysis on your own, without prompting on all of the relevant components. Perform an independent samples t-test to see if the average agreement toward “News coverage about politics in America is biased” (biasnews, you’ve used this variable in Q1) is significantly different between people who favor or oppose the death penalty for murder (cappun), among all American adults. If you write a notation with a generic subscript (e.g., $\mu_1$, $\bar{X}_2$), explain what the notation means in text. Make sure to evaluate all relevant assumptions and components. If any component is unnecessary, you should mention it and provide a brief explanation.

**4. (10 points)** This question does not require Jamovi. In a certain metropolitan area, the average number of text messages sent per day by adults is 40, with a standard deviation of 35.

\medskip
**(a)** If we randomly sample 30 adults from this population and calculate their average number of daily text messages, what would be the shape, mean, and standard deviation (also called the standard error) of the distribution of this average?


\medskip
**(b)** What is the probability that the average number of text messages for the 30 randomly sampled adults is more than 50?


\newpage

**5. (15 points)** This question does not require the use of Jamovi. The following information are adopted from a journal article “Boston Marathon athlete performance outcomes and intra-event medical encounter risk associated with low energy availability indicators.”

**Objective:** To determine the association between survey-based self-reported problematic low energy availability indicators (LEA-I) and race performance and intra-event medical encounters during the Boston Marathon.

**Methods:** 1030 runners who were registered for the 2022 Boston Marathon completed an electronic survey (1-4 weeks pre-race) assessing LEA-I, training and medical history. De-identified survey data were linked to event wearable timing chips and medical encounter records. LEA-I was defined as: an elevated Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire score, elevated Low Energy Availability (LEA) in Females Questionnaire score, LEA in Males Questionnaire with a focus on gonadal dysfunction score and/or self-report of diagnosed eating disorder/disordered eating.

**Results:** The prevalence of LEA-I was 232/546 (42.5%) in females and 85/484 (17.6%) in males. Athletes without LEA-I (non-LEA-I) achieved significantly better race times versus those with LEA-I (accounting for demographic and anthropomorphic data, training history and marathon experience), along with better division finishing place (DFP) mean outcomes (women's DFP: 948.9±57.6 versus 1377.4±82.9, p<0.001; men's DFP: 794.6±41.0 versus 1262.4±103.3, p<0.001). Compared with non-LEA-I athletes, LEA-I athletes had 1.99-fold (95% CI: 1.15 to 3.43) increased relative risk (RR) of an intra-event medical encounter of any severity level, and a 2.86-fold increased RR (95% CI:1.31 to 6.24) of a major medical encounter.

\medskip
**(a)** Multiple places in the Results section mention “p<0.001.” What does p here refer to? Why is it important to mention that “p<0.001” for a stated conclusion?


\medskip
**(b)** To compare race performance (in terms of finishing time, for instance) between non-LEA-I and LEA-I athletes, what kind of t-test, one-sample, paired samples, or independent samples, would be the most appropriate?



\medskip
**(c)** Suppose a regression analysis was performed to predict race time (in minute), and LEA-I was used as a dichotomous predictor (coded as 0=non-LEA-I and 1=LEA-I). The slope of the predictor is estimated to be 12.5. Interpret this value in the context of the problem using language that someone who hasn’t taken statistics would understand. If it is not meaningful to interpret the slope, explain why not.
